paper_title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Consider the meerkat (Figure 1). You may have recorded it on recent holiday and are watching it now on your high-resolution screen. While you admire the sharp details of the meerkat, you find the background leaves distracting and regret not having recorded the video at shallower depth of field. Applications that synthetically blur the background could help, but to reliably separate the meerkat from its background, they require depth map for every frame (Bertalmío et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2022). Picking suitable method for estimating depth from monocular videos is surprisingly difficult. Methods designed for single images can provide high-resolution depth maps with sharp occlusion boundaries. InfiniDepth (Yu et al., 2026), for instance, reasonably delineates the fur (third column of Figure 1). Yet its predictions are temporally inconsistent as it processes each frame separately and places the meerkat at different distances over time. method designed for video, such as π3 (Wang et al., 2026b), reliably places the meerkat at consistent distance across frames (last column of Figure 1). But it operates at lower resolution than the input video, which smooths over the fur. This trade-off between sharp boundaries and temporal consistency pervades monocular depth estimation. Figure 2 presents the state of the art on boundary sharpness and temporal consistency, measured over the Sintel and Spring datasets (Butler et al., 2012; Mehl et al., 2023). (We choose these datasets for their dense, high-resolution ground truth on video sequences.) We find that single-image methods cluster at the top left and multi-frame methods cluster at the bottom right. That is, depth maps from single-image methods feature the sharpest boundaries but are unstable over time, while depth maps from multi-frame methods are stable but overly smooth. Multi-frame approaches are commonly optimized for stability through temporal attention over many frames (Wang et al., 2025a, 2026b), video diffusion priors (Hu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026), and video training data (Wang et al., 2023). This biases the methods towards longer temporal context and costly diffusion, which require substantial resources (memory and runtime) and necessitate operating at reduced resolution, thus oversmoothing boundaries. In this paper, we present Depth Pro 2, method that estimates sharp, metric, and temporally consistent depth from monocular images and video. Depth Pro 2 outperforms both single-image and multi-frame 1 Input Depth Pro 2 InfiniDepth π3 Figure 1 Left to right: two frames from video (Pexels, 2026) with depth maps produced by Depth Pro 2 (our approach), InfiniDepth (Yu et al., 2026), and π3 (Wang et al., 2026b). InfiniDepth recovers fur but at inconsistent depth. π3 is temporally consistent but blurs boundaries. Depth Pro 2 delivers fine details and consistent depth between frames. Note the insets. methods in boundary sharpness and temporal consistency (see Figure 2), as well as in metric depth accuracy (see Section 4). The key idea is an architecture that processes flexible number of frames jointly at their native resolution. The joint processing stabilizes depth temporally. Operating at native resolution preserves sharp boundaries. In contrast to training with complex multi-stage curricula (Chen et al., 2025; Chou et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023), we train Depth Pro 2 on clips of 1 to 32 frames, mixing image, video, and multi-view datasets. By training on single images alongside video, Depth Pro 2 learns to infer metric scale from individual frames. By training on videos with temporal consistency loss, it learns to keep its estimates stable across frames. Depth Pro 2 predicts inverse depth normalized by the focal length, and uses the focal length of input images to recover metric depth (Bochkovskii et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2023a). To reliably estimate metric depth when the focal length is not provided, we train focal length estimator, following Depth Pro (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). In contrast to Depth Pro, however, we design our focal length estimator to be lightweight to facilitate streaming video processing. Our focal length estimator runs at 118 fps at 1080p on B200 and is more accurate than prior estimators. To support broad set of applications that may vary in the relative importance of accuracy and latency, we release family of models ranging from 24M to 872M parameters. In the streaming setting, where frames arrive one at time, our smallest model (Depth Pro 2-S) runs at 53 fps at 1080p on B200 (Figure 12), faster than the 30 fps at which most videos are recorded. Our largest model (Depth Pro 2-H+) runs at 8 fps 2 on 1080p video and outperforms all prior work in terms of metric depth, boundary sharpness, and temporal consistency, on both images and video (Section 4).

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Zero-shot metric depth. Early work trained on single-domain datasets with known camera intrinsics for domain-specific metric depth prediction (Eigen et al., 2014; Eigen & Fergus, 2015; Liu et al., 2016). Ranftl et al. (2022, 2021) pioneered training on diverse cross-domain mixtures of datasets for generalist monocular depth estimation. While this substantially increased generality and enabled zero-shot deployment across domains, their formulation relaxed the estimated depth from metric to relative. Subsequent work focused on recovering metric depth while retaining strong generalist performance (Yin et al., 2023b,a). One line of work developed approaches for handling arbitrary camera models (Piccinelli et al., 2024, 2025b,a). Another predicted point clouds to supervise via depth-affine losses (Wang et al., 2025c,d; Kong et al., 2026). MetricAnything pretrained on large-scale diverse depth completion to forego reasoning about camera intrinsics (Ma et al., 2026). Depth Pro demonstrated strong metric depth estimation through separate field-of-view estimator, which can be trained without any depth supervision (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). We build on the Depth Pro approach and train lightweight field-of-view estimator that outperforms prior work while substantially reducing the estimators size to enable accurate field-of-view and metric depth estimation at high frame rates. Sharp depth. line of work processes images in tiles at multiple scales to obtain sharper depth predictions (Bochkovskii et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024a,b, 2026; Miangoleh et al., 2021). Kong et al. (2026) lift point estimates into sparse voxels and apply sparse 3D convolutions to iteratively refine local geometry and sharpness. Yu et al. (2026) represent depth as neural implicit field that can be queried at arbitrary resolution, but require sparse metric depth as additional input to predict dense metric depth. He et al. (2026); Ke et al. (2024); Pavlovic et al. (2026) leverage latent diffusion priors and synthetic training data for predicting sharp depth boundaries. To avoid artifacts from decoding latents, Xu et al. (2025) denoise in pixel space through cascade of diffusion transformers. In contrast to prior work that combines multiple scales or iteratively refines predictions, Depth Pro 2 predicts sharp boundaries at native resolution via single pass through vision transformer. Figure 2 Sharpness versus temporal consistency. Depth Pro 2 outperforms prior work operating on single frame or multiple frames in terms of sharpness (Boundary F1 score (Bochkovskii et al., 2025)) and temporal consistency (Jitter, Sec. F.1). Results averaged over Sintel and Spring. Stable depth. Single-image methods are inconsistent when applied to individual video frames separately. To produce consistent depth maps over video sequences, researchers have proposed specialized modules (Piccinelli et al., 2026; Chou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2019), plug-and-play stabilization (Wang et al., 2023), and spatiotemporal heads (Chen et al., 2025). Another line of work fine-tunes video diffusion models for temporally consistent depth prediction (Hu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b), or adapts them into deterministic single-step regressors (Zhang et al., 2026). Instead of relying on custom modules or computationally heavy video diffusion priors, we adapt single-image vision transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) to handle flexible number of frames and penalize inconsistency between predictions during training. Another line of work takes inspiration from classic 3D reconstruction and optimizes depth jointly with camera poses (Wang et al., 2024, 2025a, 2026a,b; Lin et al., 2026). To improve the consistency of reconstructed geometry, these methods are commonly optimized for handling large sets of views, which in turn limits their ability to process images at high resolution, key requirement for producing sharp depth maps. In contrast, Depth Pro 2 estimates metric depth from flexible number of input frames and processes them at native resolution to produce significantly sharper occlusion boundaries. To enable processing of multiple images, we simply adapt subset of the self-attention layers of our transformer to attend over tokens from multiple views without introducing additional parameters. Variants of this idea have been used in video transformers (Bertasius et al., 2021; Arnab et al., 2021), multi-view recognition (Chen et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2025), and generation (Khachatryan et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024). Most closely related, Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2026) rearranges tokens so that pretrained DINOv2 attention operates across views for feedforward reconstruction. Unlike these approaches, we design our network to predict metric depth at native resolution.

sections.title: 3.1 Architecture
sections.content: Overview. The architecture of Depth Pro 2 is depicted in Fig. 3. It consists of multi-view transformer that ingests single image or multiple frames of video, processes them jointly, and decodes them to an inverse depth map per input image or video frame. Following Depth Pro, our depth estimation network predicts inverse depth normalized by focal length, and we combine it with known or estimated focal length to predict metric depth (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). separate field-of-view estimator processes the input image(s) and predicts the field-of-view per image, which we convert to the focal length. If the focal length is known priori, e.g., through EXIF data, we use that instead of running the field-of-view estimator. Lightweight multi-frame depth estimation network. We design our depth estimation network to be lightweight and to flexibly handle variable number of images, starting from ViT variant pretrained for single-image processing (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Siméoni et al., 2026). Since temporal stability requires an architecture that aligns predictions across frames, our model shares information across jointly processed frames via cross-attention, alternating blocks of within-frame self-attention and cross-frame attention (Wang et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2026). (See Fig. 3, 1 .) Since early blocks in multi-view transformers tend to encode low-level features and only later blocks approximate feature matching (Starý et al., 2026), we restrict the first 1/3 of the transformer blocks to self-attention operating only over tokens from the same frame for higher efficiency. The remaining 2L/3 blocks alternate between withinand cross-frame attention. When encoding spatial positions of tokens processed by the transformer, we specifically omit any encoding of frame order, making our network equivariant to frame permutation. This allows flexible processing of any number of frames and directly reusing the attention weights from single-image pretrained encoder checkpoints (Lin et al., 2026) without adding transformer blocks that need to be trained from scratch for multi-view processing. Native resolution processing. Boundary sharpness correlates with the resolution at which frames are processed (Miangoleh et al., 2021; Bochkovskii et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). We therefore design Depth Pro 2 to operate at the full native resolution of the input image or video. To this end, we initialize our multiview transformer from DINOv3 weights, as DINOv3 is trained specifically to produce dense, high-resolution features (Siméoni et al., 2026). An input image is split into patches of size 16, and each patch is embedded as token. We encode each tokens spatial position through 2D rotary embedding over their coordinates. Instead of normalizing coordinates per axis (Siméoni et al., 2026), which would discard any information about the images aspect ratio, we divide both axes by the longer side. The position (x, y) of patch (i, j) within grid of size is thus = 2(i + 1 2 )/ max(h, w) 1, = 2(j + 2 )/ max(h, w) 1. DPT decoder. DPT decoder (Ranftl et al., 2021) decodes features extracted per frame into inverse depth maps. (See Fig. 3, 2 .) Following DPT, we extract tokens after several transformer blocks, assemble them into feature maps at different resolutions, and project them to common channel dimension. Depending on the size of the multi-view transformer, we adjust the positions at which we extract features, and scale the 4 Figure 3 Depth Pro 2 Architecture. Our depth estimation network consists of multi-view transformer that ingests one or multiple input frames and processes them jointly, and DPT decoder, which predicts an inverse depth map per input frame. 1 The transformer alternates attention within and across frames. 2 Features for fusion by the DPT decoder are extracted at intermediate layers. Table 1 details layer configurations for each model of the Depth Pro 2 family. number of channel dimensions the decoder operates on. See Table 1 for the exact specification. To upsample feature maps within the decoder, we replace bilinear upsampling with transposed convolutions (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). Focal length estimation. Our multi-view transformer predicts inverse depth normalized by the focal length (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). Converting this prediction to metric depth therefore requires the focal length. The focal length is often recorded in EXIF metadata; when it is not, we estimate it with separate, lightweight vision transformer. This estimator predicts the field of view along the shorter image side, from which the focal length follows given the length of that side in pixels. To minimize the overhead, we build the estimator on DINOv3 ViT-S/16 (Siméoni et al., 2026) and fine-tune it end-to-end on Flickr photographs with EXIF focal lengths (Thomee et al., 2016). The estimator has 23.5M parameters and, for 1080p frame, adds about 8%, 3%, 1%, and 0.5% to the compute of Depth Pro 2-S, Depth Pro 2-B, Depth Pro 2-L, and Depth Pro 2-H+, respectively. For multi-view input, we assume constant focal length and take the median of the per-frame estimates. On the zero-shot benchmark of Bochkovskii et al. (2025), our estimator attains mean δ25 of 88.6%, compared to 71.7% for Depth Pro  (Table 6)  . Appendix A.2 describes the training setup, Appendix E.4 analyzes design choices, and Table 6 compares the estimator to prior work.

sections.title: 3.2 Training
sections.content: Training data. Depth Pro 2 is trained on diverse set of 19 datasets with strong focus on synthetic ground truth. See Table 7 for the full list. To preserve the sharpness of ground-truth depth maps, we avoid any interpolation of ground-truth depth during training, as averaging over depth discontinuities breeds flying pixels (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). To expose our model to broad set of image sizes and aspect ratios, we crop and sample images at varying strides. During training, we use ground-truth camera intrinsics (focal length) and adjust accordingly depending on how we crop or subsample. Controlled experiments in the supplement (Section E) show that training without resampling improves boundary accuracy by more than 5 percentage points over Depth Pros resizing. To handle both images and video, Depth Pro 2 is trained on clips with varying length, of which all frames are processed jointly. Images are treated as clips of length 1; for video and multi-view datasets, clip contains up to 32 frames. (We use frame for both video frames and views.) For each clip, we draw the source dataset with probability pi n1/T , where ni is the size of dataset and = 2 (Arivazhagan et al., 2019). To avoid 5 overfitting to small datasets, we cap their sampling weight. Batching. To efficiently train with varying resolutions and clip lengths, we batch by tokens. Each GPU receives fixed budget of 73,728 tokens, e.g., 18 frames at 1024 1024. When clip leaves part of the budget unused, we fill the remainder with further clips of the same resolution. Training objective. Our loss is the unweighted sum of four terms: = Lmae + Lssi + Lmge + Lmvc. (3.1) Lmae is trimmed L1 loss on focal-normalized inverse depth. It anchors metric depth, and we apply it only to sources with metric ground truth. sections.title: 3.3 Inference
sections.content: Depth Pro 2 is trained on clips of up to 32 frames but at inference time processes videos of arbitrary length. It supports two modes. Buffered streaming accumulates frames into clips and processes each clip with full attention across its frames. Unbuffered streaming produces depth map for each frame as soon as it arrives, for applications that require minimal latency. Buffered streaming. For buffered streaming, we divide the video into clips of frames, with consecutive clips overlapping by frames, and process each clip independently. The overlap keeps predictions consistent across clip boundaries. Within the overlap, we blend the two predictions with weights that change linearly with frame position. Section E.3 reports controlled experiments on the choice of and K. Unbuffered streaming. Unbuffered streaming minimizes per-frame latency. In this mode, Depth Pro 2 processes frames sequentially with causal cross-attention: each frame attends only to itself and to preceding frames. The keys and values of past frames remain fixed as new frames arrive, so we compute them once and keep them in first-in-first-out (FIFO) cache. Each frame attends to window of frames: itself and the 1 frames before it, the keys and values of which are cached. Only the cross-frame attention layers use this cache; the per-frame layers operate on the current frame alone.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: In addition to the experiments and results reported in this section, the supplement provides model and training details (Appendix A), further quantitative and qualitative comparisons to prior work (Appendix B), an evaluation of the Depth Pro 2 model family (Appendix C), evaluations on downstream applications (Appendix D), controlled experiments including an evaluation on long video sequences (Appendix E), and specification of the evaluation protocols (Appendix F). We evaluate Depth Pro 2 in zero-shot settings on metric depth accuracy, boundary sharpness, and temporal consistency, comparing against comprehensive set of baselines. When comparing to prior work in Tables 25, we use Depth Pro 2-H+. Figure 4 provides qualitative comparison to prior work. For further qualitative assessment, we encourage the reader to watch the videos at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/. Zero-shot metric depth. We evaluate Depth Pro 2 for zero-shot metric depth accuracy against singleimage and multi-image baselines that predict dense metric depth. We report results on iBims (Koch et al., 2018), Middlebury (Scharstein et al., 2014), Booster (Ramirez et al., 2022), HAMMER (Jung et al., 2023), ETH3D (Schöps et al., 2017), KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012), NuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020), DIODE (Vasiljevic et al., 2019), Sintel (Butler et al., 2012), Spring (Mehl et al., 2023), and DyDToF (Sun et al., 2023). Ten datasets are adopted from the evaluation sets of Depth Pro (Bochkovskii et al., 2025) and MoGe-3 (Kong et al., 2026). We add DyDToF, synthetic video dataset with dense metric ground truth and sharp boundaries. These datasets have been excluded from the training data for most methods and are therefore ideal for zeroshot benchmarking. Baselines that do not conform to the zero-shot setting are marked in gray. We do not include datasets captured with Kinect sensors due to noisy, biased, and incomplete ground truth. For fair comparison of single-image and video methods, we evaluate them in dedicated single-image and video settings. In the single-image setting  (Table 2)  , all methods are run and evaluated per frame. In the video setting  (Table 3)  , we use the datasets that provide video frames (KITTI, Sintel, Spring, and DyDToF). Every method receives the same clips of 50 frames. Single-image methods process each frame independently. All of our subsequent zero-shot evaluations follow this split as well. ETH3D is multi-view stereo benchmark with wide-baseline views of static scene rather than video, so it appears in the single-image setting only. We evaluate all models under two conditions: first with ground-truth camera intrinsics and second with predicted camera intrinsics, if the model is capable of estimating focal length. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented family of models that estimate sharp and temporally consistent metric depth. By analyzing prior approaches to monocular depth estimation, we observed dichotomy between image-based methods that produce sharp depth maps and video-based methods that are temporally stable but elide detail. Depth Pro 2 overcomes this trade-off and provides unprecedented sharpness and temporal stability. We release family of models, each of which processes both single images and video sequences at full resolution, and can process video in streaming fashion. The smallest model, Depth Pro 2-S, processes streaming 1080p video at 53 fps on single GPU. The largest model, Depth Pro 2-H+, processes 1080p video at 8 fps and sets the new state of the art on metric depth accuracy, boundary sharpness, and temporal stability all at once.

sections.title: Supplement
sections.content: This supplement is organized as follows. Appendix provides implementation and training details. Appendix provides additional qualitative and quantitative results. Appendix provides quantitative comparison between different models in the Depth Pro 2 family. Appendix evaluates predicted depth in two downstream applications: bokeh rendering and novel-view synthesis. Appendix presents controlled experiments and examines design choices and parameter settings. Appendix specifies the evaluation protocol used throughout the paper, including the held-out validation sets and how we measure runtime.

sections.title: A Implementation details
sections.content: A.1 Training Training optimization. We train all our models for 100K steps on 128 B200 GPUs. We use AdamW at peak learning rate of 5 105, cosine annealed after 5% warmup. Section 3.2 describes our native-resolution training strategy. Here, we provide additional implementation details on token-budget batching and the composition of the training data. Token-budget batching. Each GPU has maximum budget of 73,728 patch tokens during training. Half of the steps use the full native frame. Otherwise, we draw an aspect ratio relative to the native aspect and short-side limit, then crop to 60100% of the largest feasible window. Where native resolution permits, we choose spatial stride 2 with probability 0.25, taking every second pixel in both the image and depth. We do not interpolate ground truth to keep fidelity. Each clip uses as many frames as fit in the token budget, up to separate cap of 32 frames. Remaining capacity is filled with more clips from the same source. The short side of the input video is 608/1024/2048 pixels at 10th/50th/90th percentiles. The sampled aspect ratios are 1.00/1.07/1.50 at the same percentiles. Loss application and normalization. We apply Lssi to all data sources. For metric synthetic and real sensor sources, we apply Lmae . We in addition apply Lmge on dense synthetic depth, and Lmvc on multi-frame sources with camera poses. For Lssi and Lmae , we first average over valid pixels within each frame, then average over frames per GPU. For Lmge , we pool valid pixels across frames separately at each pyramid level and weight the levels equally. For Lmvc, we average over sampled valid pixel pairs from frame pairs. Gradients are averaged equally across GPUs. Training datasets. Table 7 lists each dataset used for training, whether it contains real or synthetic images, the number of scenes, total frames, and the maximum resolution of frames within the dataset. In addition to publicly available datasets, we include internal real-world and synthetic data. Internal (Real) consists of handheld smartphone videos with time-of-flight depth labels and camera poses. Internal (Synthetic) features humans, pets, and objects in rendered indoor and outdoor environments under varied lighting in static and dynamic scenes, rendered from multiple viewpoints and with moving cameras. Images are supplemented with dense metric depth, intrinsics, and extrinsics. A.2 Field-of-view estimation Architecture. We initialize our field-of-view estimator with pretrained DINOv3 ViT-S/16, and finetune end-to-end on ImageNet-normalized inputs. small attention head (1.9M parameters, two transformer blocks of width 248) reads the tokens of blocks 2, 5, 8, and 11, and predicts the horizontal and vertical fields of view, each bounded to [1, 179]. Training. We train on large corpus of 92M images from Flickr (Thomee et al., 2016), discarding those with invalid or missing EXIF data. Augmentation and input size. We resize every image to 512 pixels along its shorter side, retaining original aspect ratios. Augmentations comprise horizontal flips (p = 0.5) and standard photometric changes (color removal or jitter, blur, noise, JPEG/WebP recompression). the Temporal Alignment Error (TAE), and report results in Table 12. This evaluation uses the Spring (Mehl et al., 2023), Sintel (Butler et al., 2012), ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017), Bonn (Palazzolo et al., 2019), and KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) datasets. TAE differs from our jitter metric (Section F.1) in the computation of correspondences. While jitter relies on track-based correspondences that account for dynamic objects, TAE reprojects predicted depth between consecutive frames using the ground-truth camera intrinsics and poses, and measures the resulting absolute relative error (Yang et al., 2025b). TAE assumes static scene and does not account for independently moving objects. TAE is ambiguous at occlusions, which can result in non-zero TAE for ground-truth depth and predictions that attain lower errors than the ground truth, demonstrated in Table 12. Further non-zero TAE for groundtruth depth can stem from imprecise depth annotations (e.g., from Kinect sensor), meaning methods may be penalized for better depth coverage. (We define jitter relative to the ground truth, which circumvents this problem.) On Sintel and Spring, the depth annotations are sufficiently dense and high-quality that we compute mask to exclude dynamic content and occlusions, whereas the depth of ScanNet, Bonn, and KITTI is sparse and/or low-quality. We evaluate depth-guided bokeh rendering, where depth errors near object boundaries produce visible foregroundbackground blending artifacts. We hold the renderer fixed and vary only its input depth, thereby evaluating the downstream utility of each estimator rather than comparing end-to-end bokeh-generation systems. We use the 220 test scenes from RealBokeh (Seizinger et al., 2025), each containing an /22 source image and corresponding real /2 photograph. For each source image, we estimate metric depth and provide inverse metric depth to frozen BokehMe renderer (Peng et al., 2022). For Depth Pro 2, we convert focal-normalized disparity using its predicted focal length; baselines are converted according to their native metric representations. We apply no depth renormalization or per-image alignment. Non-metric methods are excluded because their missing scale and shift cannot be recovered without scene-specific fitting. We also exclude MetricAnything, which requires supplied focal length to produce metric depth, whereas no camera intrinsics are provided to any method in this study. All images are rendered and evaluated at 20001500 resolution. The renderer and all its parameters are fixed across methods, including one global disparity multiplier selected on disjoint validation set of 60 scenes. No parameters are fitted on the test set. Boundary LPIPS. In addition to full-image PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), and DISTS (Ding et al., 2022), we measure LPIPS within 16-pixel band around the captures defocus boundaries. This band is derived solely from the /22 source and /2 target images and is therefore identical across methods. We first exposure-align the target luma to the source using global affine least-squares fit. For each image, we compute local high-frequency energy as = box15((2ℓ)2). Pixels whose source energy exceeds its 60th percentile are classified as in focus when ρ = Etgt/(Etgt + Esrc) 0.25. We close the resulting mask with 9-pixel elliptical element, retain its largest 8-connected component, and fill its holes. Boundary LPIPS is the mean spatial LPIPS within eight pixels of the resulting boundary on either side, obtained using an exact Euclidean distance transform. Results. Depth Pro 2-H+ performs best across all five metrics. Relative to Depth Anything 3-NGL at 504 378, the strongest baseline on four of the five metrics, it improves PSNR by 0.50 dB and reduces global and Boundary LPIPS by 4.9% and 5.6%, respectively. Relative to Depth Pro, it improves PSNR by 0.75 dB and reduces the two LPIPS measures by 8.8% and 10.1%. These results indicate that the metric depth and camera calibration produced by Depth Pro 2 provide more effective guidance near defocus boundaries. This single-image benchmark does not assess temporal consistency. Video. We additionally apply the frozen renderer frame by frame to 197-frame handheld clip from Pexels (2026). At 128 GPUs, every metric improves monotonically with model size, from Depth Pro 2-S (B1) to Depth Pro 2-H+ (B4). Training data. Our training data combine external datasets and internal data, and both contain synthetic and real-world parts. We vary this mix in four ways: adding real-world data (D1), removing all real-world data (D2), removing all external data (D3), and removing all internal data (D4). D1 adds Objectron (Ahmadyan et al., 2021), Argoverse2 (Wilson et al., 2021), MapFree (Arnold et al., 2022), the training sequences of ARKitScenes (Dehghan et al., 2021), WayveScenes101 (Zürn et al., 2024), TartanRGBT (Maheshwari et al., 2026), the Aria captures (ADT (Pan et al., 2023), HOT3D (Banerjee et al., 2025), Nymeria (Ma et al., 2024), and Reading in the Wild (Yang et al., 2025a)), and additional internal real-world captures. Adding real-world data (D1) improves depth accuracy but smooths boundaries. We attribute the smoothing to the ground truth of real-world datasets, which comes from depth sensors and is often inaccurate at occlusion 33 boundaries. Consistent with this, removing all real-world data (D2) sharpens boundaries beyond the baseline but degrades depth accuracy. Training on internal data only (D3) degrades every metric. Removing all internal data (D4) improves accuracy on Waymo, sharpens boundaries, and lowers jitter, but lowers metric δ1 on ARKitScenes by 45.2 percentage points. Internal data thus improves generalization to ARKitScenes, the one validation dataset outside the training mix, at some cost in boundary sharpness and temporal consistency. Training resolution. The baseline (A1) trains on crops of any aspect ratio at native scale and subsamples some crops with stride of 2, which adds lower-resolution views without interpolating the ground truth. Removing the strided subsampling (E1) slightly improves accuracy but degrades boundary sharpness. Training only on square crops at native scale (E2) preserves most of the sharpness but lowers metric δ1 on Waymo by 46.6 percentage points. Waymo frames have aspect ratios of 3:2 and about 2.2:1, which suggests that the model needs varied aspect ratios and fields of view in training to recover metric scale. Resizing the square crops to 1536 1536, as Depth Pro (Bochkovskii et al., 2025) does (E3), lowers boundary sharpness further, consistent with the benefit of training at native resolution. Backbone. Replacing the pretrained DINOv3 backbone with DINOv2 ViT-L/14 (H1) slightly lowers jitter but lowers metric δ1 on ARKitScenes by 12.8 points. Freezing DINOv3 (H2) degrades every metric. Training losses. Removing the multi-view consistency loss (I1) raises jitter by 0.05. Replacing our gradient loss with the first-order boundary loss of Depth Pro (I2), which computes the same gradient error at 6 scales instead of 3, lowers boundary F1 by 3.5 percentage points. The full set of Depth Pro boundary losses (I3), which adds second-order and squared-gradient terms to I2, lowers boundary F1 by 3.8 percentage points and lowers metric δ1 on Waymo by 3.3 points. Weighting our inverse-depth losses by predicted confidence (I4), as feed-forward reconstruction methods do, lowers boundary F1 by 6.8 points. We hypothesize that the model is least certain at boundaries, so confidence weighting lets it discount the loss exactly where it must learn to resolve them. F.2 Zero-shot evaluation details Zero-shot status. We show result in gray when the evaluated checkpoint was trained on the evaluation dataset. Gray entries are excluded from the per-dataset ranks and from the average ranks across datasets, so the average rank of method with gray entries covers only the datasets on which it is zero-shot. Single-image and video settings. Depth Pro 2 accepts both single frames and multi-frame clips, as do several baselines. Most other baselines accept only single images. DepthCrafter, VeloDepth and Video Depth Anything accept only clips, and VeloDepth reduces to UniK3D on single frame. To compare both kinds of method fairly, we evaluate metric depth and boundary sharpness in two settings. In the single-image setting, every method receives one frame at time. On video and multi-view datasets, we predict and score each of the first 50 frames of sequence as separate image, and methods estimate the focal length for every frame independently. In the video setting, every method receives the first 50 frames of sequence as one clip. Video methods process the clip jointly, and single-image methods process its frames independently. We evaluate temporal consistency in the video setting only. The boundary metric of Bochkovskii et al. (2025) and our temporal-consistency metrics are scale-invariant, so we also evaluate methods that predict only relative depth on them. Baseline evaluation. We evaluate all baselines from their released checkpoints with the protocols in this section, unless noted otherwise. Our scores may differ from published results, because studies differ in camera intrinsics, alignment procedures, sampled frames or sequences, and evaluation resolution. Evaluation splits. Lin et al. (2026) and Piccinelli et al. (2025a) evaluate on the indoor split of DIODE (Vasiljevic et al., 2019) only. We evaluate on the full validation split, indoor and outdoor. The outdoor scenes are harder, so our DIODE scores are lower than those reported on the indoor split. We use the official DIODE validity mask for every metric. For nuScenes, we use the evaluation split of Bochkovskii et al. (2025), and for HAMMER, the split of Kong et al. (2026). Both splits consist of individual frames, so we evaluate them in the single-image setting only. F.3 Baseline configurations Common input. We evaluate every method on the same frames: one contiguous clip of the first 50 frames per video sequence, sampled at stride one. Prior work samples frames, sets clip lengths, and aligns predictions in different ways, so published video-depth results are hard to compare directly. For example, VGGT-Ω evaluates 10 randomly sampled frames per sequence (Wang et al., 2026a, 4). Video Depth Anything 38 evaluates up to 500 frames per video, reports 90and 110-frame settings for comparison with DepthCrafter, and aligns predictions in inverse-depth space (Chen et al., 2025). The one exception to our common input is the temporal alignment evaluation on ScanNet  (Table 12)  , where we use the 170-frame clips of the Video Depth Anything evaluation (Chen et al., 2025). Clip processing. Each method processes the clip with its official inference procedure. Methods that accept 50 frames receive the whole clip in one pass; the others use their released windowing, e.g., Video Depth Anything processes 32-frame windows. On ScanNet, Depth Pro 2-H+ runs in buffered streaming with clips of = 64 frames and an overlap of = 32. Input resolution. We retain each methods official inference resolution because changing it can affect metric accuracy, boundary sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. For example, Depth Pro resizes every frame to 1536 1536. Some methods crop the input in their official preprocessing (e.g., VGGT-Ω). For these methods, we pad each frame so that the crop removes only padding, and then remove the padding from the prediction. Every method is thus evaluated on the same image region. Output resizing. Because methods differ in their internal preprocessing, their predictions may not match the spatial resolution of the ground truth. In such cases, we resize the prediction to the ground-truth resolution using nearest-neighbor interpolation, thereby avoiding additional smoothing at depth discontinuities. Affine alignment. Before computing relative-depth accuracy, boundary F1, and temporal consistency, we align each prediction to the ground truth with scale and shift. We align every method this way, including metric-depth models and Depth Pro 2, so that these metrics measure the structure of prediction independently of its metric scale. For relative-depth accuracy (Tables 10 and 11) and boundary F1  (Table 4)  , we fit the scale and shift for each frame separately, also when method predicts the frames of clip jointly. For jitter  (Table 5)  and TAE  (Table 12)  , we fit one scale and shift per video, which preserves the variation in scale across frames that these metrics measure. By default, we fit the scale and shift in inverse-depth space by trimmed least squares: we keep the 80% of sampled valid pixels with the smallest squared residuals. Three methods output log depth (Lapis, PixelPerfect Depth, and Marigold V2). Following their evaluation protocols, we fit these methods in log-depth space with the same trimming. Tables 4(a), 4(b), and 5 mark them with (log). F.4 Held-out validation The controlled experiments (Appendix E), the inference-time analysis studies (Appendix E.2), and the longvideo evaluation (Appendix E.3) use held-out validation sequences from three datasets that do not appear in the zero-shot evaluation: Waymo (Sun et al., 2020) (real, outdoor; 42 sequences at 1280 1920 or 886 1920), ARKitScenes (Dehghan et al., 2021) (real, indoor; 92 sequences at 14401920), and DynamicReplica (Karaev et al., 2023) (synthetic; 44 sequences at 720 1280). We train on the training sequences of Waymo and DynamicReplica, and on those of ARKitScenes only in condition D1 of the controlled experiments. Conditions D2 and D3 leave out Waymo and D3 also DynamicReplica. We hold out 5% of the data shards of each dataset from training, selected by fixed hash. Of the 46 held-out DynamicReplica sequences, we discard two in which the camera passes through scene geometry: over part of each sequence, the ground truth contains surface few centimeters from the camera that the image does not show. From each sequence, we take one window of up to 32 consecutive frames, starting at seeded random frame, and process it in single forward pass, at native resolution unless study varies the input size. The long-video evaluation instead uses the first 300 frames of each sequence. We report four metrics: metric δ1 with the ground-truth focal length; relative δ1 after per-frame affine fit in inverse-depth space; the boundary F1 of Bochkovskii et al. (2025); and, on DynamicReplica, jitter (Eq. F.1) along point tracks obtained by chaining the ground-truth optical flow. F.5 Runtime measurement Setup. We measure the runtime of Depth Pro 2 in Figures 10 and 12 with our code release on one B200 GPU, in eager PyTorch without torch.compile, with cuDNN attention (the PyTorch default on this GPU). The backbone and decoder run under bf16 autocast, and the depth head runs in fp32. The inputs are synthetic 16:9 frames. The focal length is given, so the field-of-view network is excluded from the timings. Each configuration, defined by the model, the input size, and and or C, runs in its own process. We run each configuration 3 times and report the median across runs. Timing. We time two operations: buffered pass over clip of frames, and an unbuffered step with full cache of frames. Each time is the median of 20 calls after 2 warm-up calls. Latency and throughput follow from these times. Latency. Latency is the time from the arrival of frame from 30 fps camera to the availability of its depth map. In unbuffered streaming, each frame is processed on arrival, so its latency is the time of one step. This assumes that the GPU is idle when the frame arrives, which holds when throughput is at least 30 fps; at lower throughput, the frames of live camera queue up or must be dropped. Throughput. Throughput is the number of frames finalized per second on long video. In buffered streaming, each pass finalizes frames, so throughput is divided by the time of one pass. In unbuffered streaming, it is one divided by the time of one step. Peak memory. Peak memory is the maximum memory reserved by PyTorchs caching allocator while processing video, over one warm-up pass and three timed passes. In buffered streaming, the video spans it has 128 frames for clips of up to 64 frames and 2N frames for at least two clips, as long video does: {96, 128, 192}. The Full variant in Figure 10 uses 300 frames. In unbuffered streaming, the video has 128 frames for every cache size, since the cache is allocated in full on the first frame.
